Radar cross section (RCS) measures how much electromagnetic energy an object scatters back to the radar receiver.
Static electric polarizability relates the induced dipole moment to a static electric field.
The paper uses full-wave electromagnetic computations to estimate static polarizability from RCS.
The study focuses on dielectric spheres with radius 1 meter and relative permittivities of 2 and 10.
Normalized polarizability for a perfect conductor sphere is 3.
Rayleigh scattering approximation applies when the wavelength is much larger than the object size.
WIPL-D software was used for RCS calculations with mesh densities of 216 and 96 patches.
Symmetry planes reduced computational complexity by meshing only one fourth of the sphere.
Accuracy of polarizability estimation is about three significant digits within the valid frequency range.
Low-frequency breakdown occurs in the solver below certain frequencies depending on mesh density.
High-frequency divergence in estimates occurs around 10 MHz for a 1 meter radius sphere.
The equivalent radius of the sphere was used to approximate the surface in calculations.
The method can be extended to other shapes, such as cubes, with similar accuracy.
Polarizability is a dyadic but reduces to a scalar for symmetric objects like spheres and cubes.
The study bridges dynamic electromagnetic scattering and static electrostatics problems.
The free-space wavelength in the valid frequency range is 100 to 10,000 times the object size.
Calculation time per frequency point was about 10 seconds for the dense mesh and 2 seconds for the coarse mesh on a 1 GHz laptop.
The lowest order basis functions with two per edge were used in the mesh.
The polarizability problem is traditionally solved by Laplace equation solvers, which are computationally demanding.
The study suggests dynamic solvers can effectively estimate static polarizability despite not being designed for static calculations.
